newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Shippers hope for early end to transit cargo ban.
newsitem.headline: Shippers hope for early end to transit cargo ban.

text.p: Air cargo rates from Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport were stable over the last four weeks, but forwarders were anxiously awaiting a cancellation of a recent customs ban on transit cargo through Moscow.
"After the customs ban was enforced some clients began to use more convenient Finnish carriers for cargo," said Igor Mordvinov, senior sales manager of Burlington Air Express Moscow.
Under the ban, imposed on March 20, shippers cannot automatically forward cargo into the Russian provinces through Moscow, as every client must come to Moscow to clear customs.
Mordvinov said the market was stable in the last four weeks. "We made 40 percent more shipments in the first three months of this year compared the same period of 1996," he said.

Vladimir Yemelyanov, a spokesman for the State Customs Committee, said the transit ban was only temporary. "We have prepared new rules to cancel the ban. The head of customs should sign it soon," he said.

Boris Panchenko, senior cargo manager at forwarding firm Eruslan said the transit ban could help Western airlines operating direct cargo and passenger flights from Western Europe to provincial Russian cities.
Mordvinov said airlines might slowly increase cargo rates next month. He said cargo handling fees at Sheremetyevo might also go up soon.
"We think carriers may increase rates by 5-7 percent soon," he said, adding that rates to Tokyo has already increased 10 cents to $4.20 for 1 kg per 100 kg shipment.

Sergei Mochalov, a senior cargo manager at TCT Cargo, an Aeroflot agent, said Aeroflot had increased rates by about 30 percent on cargo routes from Moscow to Khabarovsk, Yerevan, Baku and Tbilisi earlier this month.
Forwarders said Aeroflot increased the rate to $1.60 from $1.10 per kg for a 100 kg shipment on the Moscow-Khabarovsk route.
An official at rival Transaero said that the company did not plan to increase the rates on the Moscow-Vladivostok route.
Transaero had a fixed rate of $2.90 per kg for 100 kg shipment.
"Aeroflot's rate increase is serious for clients, but not as serious as the customs ban, which has left the air cargo market stagnant," Mochalov said.
He said some companies had suffered large losses because of the customs ban. "We planned very profitable shipments and they were cancelled due to the ban," he said.
Mochalov also said Aeroflot did not plan to change its rates to top international destinations because of sharp competition.
Nadezda Sokolova, Aeroservice cargo manager, said the market was stable and could be more active over the next few weeks due to an increase in the number of cargo flights for the summer schedule.
"Almost all carriers will add scheduled cargo flights," she added.
But Natalia Titova, cargo specialist at International Transport Service Japan, said deliveries of transit cargo from Japan had stopped completely after the ban was employed.
"But we have many new clients who asked us to make customs clearance of their cargo in Moscow. It is a good business...but it is not an alternative for cargo operations," she said.

Vladimir Pavlov, a cargo manager at Soby, another Aeroflot agent, also stressed tough competition. "Sometimes forwarders give discounts of about 30 percent for its clients on international flights," he said.
Pavlov said U.S. destinations were active in the last four weeks. Sokolova said there were many shipments to Western Europe as well as to the United States, Hong Kong, China and Japan.
Mochalov at TCT Cargo said his company had stable turnover on routes between Moscow and Paris and London.
